church_lutheran.structure_note: CONFIRMED 2026-09-04: US Lutheranism is NOT one uniform polity -- the two largest bodies differ significantly, and this file is deliberately structured around BOTH variants rather than assuming one. (1) LCMS (Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod) and WELS (Wisconsin Evangelical Lutheran Synod) are explicitly CONGREGATIONAL in polity -- confirmed directly: 'the LCMS has traditionally been congregational, as opposed to hierarchical, in its extra-congregational structure.' Elected regional (district) and national leaders are deliberately titled 'President,' never 'Bishop,' specifically to avoid any suggestion of hierarchical authority. A district president may suggest pastoral candidates but 'does not assign pastors' -- the congregation itself extends the call directly, much closer to church_baptist.json's model than to industry_church_catholic.json's. (2) ELCA (Evangelical Lutheran Church in America) is genuinely different: it describes its own polity as 'modified episcopal... with some powers reserved to the congregation as in congregationalism.' Real Bishops exist at both the Synod (regional) and Churchwide (national) levels. HOWEVER, confirmed directly via the ELCA Presiding Bishop's own official public statement: 'Congregations are where most of our power -- and notably for these purposes property -- is held. Synods play an administrative and frequently pastoral role over the congregations and Churchwide plays an administrative role over all of this... [Churchwide] doesn't actually own any churches.' This means NEITHER major US Lutheran body follows TEC's Dennis-Canon-style national/diocesan property trust claim (see industry_church_episcopal.json) -- Lutheran congregations in both major bodies own their own property directly. Do not assume a Lutheran tenant's polity without first confirming which body it belongs to (ELCA, LCMS, WELS, or a smaller independent body such as LCMC or NALC, both of which split from ELCA over polity and theological disagreements and lean even more congregational than LCMS). Lutheran sacramental theology recognizes Baptism and the Lord's Supper/Eucharist as the two primary Sacraments (holding to a 'Real Presence' view of the Eucharist, distinct from both Catholic transubstantiation and the more memorial/symbolic view common in Baptist tradition) -- this specific doctrinal framing is based on well-established general knowledge, not independently re-verified with a fresh primary-source search in this pass, unlike the polity citations above.
